candidates.title: What to Admit and How to Present: Governing Persistent Memory in LLM Agents
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint, under review at AAMAS 2027
candidates.citationVelocity: published 6 days (submitted 2026-10-08); Semantic Scholar confirms 0 citations after initial 429s
communitySignals: no reproduction repo found on Papers with Code
credibilityEvidence: Section 4: dual-surface evaluation (4-backbone development suite over PersistBench dimensions n=122/91/200, external MemSyco-Bench 4 tasks x 300 samples) with McNemar tests, Holm correction on preregistered families, Benjamini-Hochberg correction on cross-backbone families

Section 4.4: three preregistration documents (cross-backbone suite; external gate and three-way comparison; verdict-shared rendering experiment) frozen before data collection and released with the paper, alongside per-sample binary labels and an independent audit script
Section 4.2: human-judge validation -- two annotators independently labeled 360 development-surface outputs, judge agrees with consensus at binary kappa=0.70
Section 6 Discussion: explicit threats-to-validity subsection naming single-judge dependence, pooled-metric interpretation caveats, and single-generator external surface as scoped limitations
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers pipeline-level comparison against verbatim injection and a reimplemented gating baseline, a verdict-shared presentation-only comparison, and a single-variable admission-tightening control, each isolating a different causal claim with its own statistical test
reproducibilityEvidence: Three preregistration documents, per-sample binary labels for every arm, and an independent audit script released with the paper; no public code repository link for the adjudication/rendering implementation found within this round's reading
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The paper's own framing (admission helps but at a personalization cost; presentation shows no robust difference; PS misses its own preregistered effect-size gate) matches the bounded claim strength used in the article
candidates.primaryLimitation: Both tested admission designs increase missed-personalization failures (FC +7.6pp, PS +5.3pp, both significant), and PS misses its own preregistered effect-size gate (needed >=10pp pooled improvement, got 8.8pp; personalization accuracy -6.0pp vs a 3pp no-degradation line)
candidates.presentationReason: Problem formulation (admission vs. presentation as two levers), method, statistical design, and a dedicated threats-to-validity section are stated with unusual explicitness
candidates.reason: First paper to decompose agent memory governance into two separately controlled, separately measured levers (admission vs. presentation) with a preregistered, dual-surface, multiply-corrected statistical design; selected over PACE and Option-Channel Attack because this round completed a full-text credibility read while those two remain abstract-only after 10 and 4 days respectively in the watch pool

candidates.title: DAYJOB: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Professional Work
candidates.venue: Early version accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Agentic AI Benchmarks and Applications for Enterprise Tasks (AABA4ET), NeurIPS 2026; current arXiv version not yet through main-conference or journal peer review
candidates.citationVelocity: published 13 days (submitted 2026-10-01); Semantic Scholar confirms 0 citations
candidates.institution: Surge AI (evaluation/data-labeling company, not an academic institution)
communitySignals: full healthcare dataset + 50/80 finance tasks public on Hugging Face (surgeai/DAYJOB-healthcare, surgeai/DAYJOB-finance)
credibilityEvidence: Section 5.1: 30 model configurations from 13 developers, 5 attempts per task on 50 healthcare + 80 finance containerized (Harbor) tasks, strict pass@1 reported with full leaderboard table
Section 5.2: relaxed-threshold analysis (90%/95%/N-1 criteria) as a robustness check against the strict all-or-nothing scoring, with Kendall tau_b rank-stability checks
Section 5.3: cost-frontier analysis against mean cost per attempt across all 30 configurations
Section 6: three concrete case studies with quoted model reasoning and quantified rubric failures (unchallenged premises, a sign error hiding a covenant breach, a data-definition mixup)
Section 3.5: three-layer professional review process for task correctness/completeness/solvability; ancillary files reproduce every statistic/table/figure
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Main results, relaxed-threshold robustness check, cost-frontier analysis, and case studies all reinforce each other and point to the same underlying failure pattern (premise-acceptance and error-propagation, not raw knowledge gaps)
reproducibilityEvidence: Evaluation harness released under Apache 2.0 (github.com/surge-ai/dayjob); all 50 healthcare tasks and 50 of 80 finance tasks public on Hugging Face under MIT license; scripts reproducing every statistic, table, and figure included as ancillary files; remaining 30 finance tasks withheld and available on request, with the training-contamination rationale stated explicitly
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The paper reports both the strict all-or-nothing score and relaxed thresholds side by side, so the article's framing ('passing everything is hard, not that models can't do this at all') is directly supported by the paper's own numbers
candidates.primaryLimitation: Currently a NeurIPS workshop (AABA4ET) accepted early version, not main-conference or journal peer-reviewed; 30 of 80 finance tasks are withheld from public release to prevent future training contamination
candidates.presentationReason: Task definition, rubric construction, evaluation protocol, and case studies are stated with concrete examples and numbers throughout; the scope of what the all-or-nothing metric does and does not capture is explicit via the relaxed-threshold companion analysis
candidates.reason: Decayed in the watch pool for 10 rounds without a full-text read (0.85^10~=0.197); given that read this round, it is the first long-horizon benchmark built from real professional documents (not plain-text Q&A) requiring every rubric criterion to pass, with full open release of the harness and most tasks -- strong enough on full-text evidence to compete with and beat its own decay

candidates.title: When Faster Decisions Do Not Make Better Agents: An Empirical Study of Jev in Agent Workflows
candidates.citationVelocity: published 5 days (submitted 2026-10-09); Semantic Scholar confirms 0 citations
candidates.institution: Nanjing University / Technical University of Munich
communitySignals: no reproduction repo found on Papers with Code
experimental code on an anonymous 4open.science link (review-purpose, not a permanent public repository)
credibilityEvidence: Section 4-5: 5 agent families (T3A, AutoDroid, FastAgent on AndroidWorld; ReAct, Reflexion on ALFWorld) x 2 benchmarks, 4,500 task executions across 3 repeated runs per configuration

Section 4.2-4.3: a dedicated LLM-Choice (C) control condition isolates 'candidate-interface change' from 'decision-model change', with paired 95% task-cluster bootstrap intervals (20,000 replicates) for all B-J/B-C/C-J comparisons
Section 5.3: systematic two-annotator trace coding of 251 codable executions into 7 binary behavior labels, pre-adjudication Cohen's kappa 0.756-1.000 per label
Table 2: resources-per-delivered-success analysis (cost/time per success including failed attempts) as the paper's core counter-metric to naive per-attempt savings
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: All three stated research questions (effectiveness, efficiency transfer, failure/recovery) are quantified with matched controls and inter-rater-validated qualitative coding, not just aggregate benchmark scores
reproducibilityEvidence: Experimental code published at an anonymous 4open.science review link; no permanent public repository or raw trace-data release found
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The paper's own title states the claim boundary (faster decisions do not make better agents), and Section 6's engineering-implications framing matches the bounded, workflow-dependent strength used in the article
candidates.primaryLimitation: Tested on only 5 agent families across 2 purely text-based benchmarks (ALFWorld, AndroidWorld), deliberately excluding visual tasks since Jev currently only accepts text input; findings about this specific, <1-month-old product may not generalize to future versions
candidates.presentationReason: Research questions, experimental design, the LLM-Choice control's purpose, and the resources-per-success framing are all stated explicitly and tied back to concrete trajectory examples
candidates.reason: First systematic third-party empirical test of a brand-new agent-component category (typed 'System One' decision models); selected over X-AgentRed (2610.13886, also carried forward from 2026-10-13) because a full-text read this round confirmed rigorous, matched-control evidence directly relevant to an active agent-engineering adoption decision, while X-AgentRed still awaits its own full-text read
